content: This updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 2011 and last updated in 2019, focuses on the use of felbamate as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder that affects approximately 1% of the population. Among these individuals, up to 30% experience seizures that are resistant to currently available antiepileptic drugs, necessitating the use of multiple medications in combination. Felbamate is a second-generation antiepileptic drug that has been proposed as an adjunctive treatment in such cases. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and tolerability of felbamate compared to placebo when used as an add-on therapy for individuals with drug-resistant focal-onset epilepsy. For the most recent update, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and MEDLINE (Ovid) up to July 13, 2021. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. Additional studies were identified by reviewing reference lists, contacting felbamate manufacturers, and consulting experts in the field. The review included randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving participants of any age with drug-resistant focal seizures. Eligible studies could employ double-blind, single-blind, or unblinded designs and could follow either a parallel-group or cross-over format. Two independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion and extracted data, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. The outcomes assessed included a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, absolute or percentage reduction in seizure frequency, treatment withdrawal rates, adverse effects, and quality of life. Four randomized controlled trials, involving a total of 236 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Two studies used a parallel-group design, one employed a two-period cross-over design, and the fourth used a three-period cross-over design. All four studies were judged to have an unclear risk of bias due to incomplete reporting of methodological details, selective reporting of outcome data, and unstable drug regimens during experimental treatment in one trial. Significant methodological and clinical heterogeneity, as well as differences in outcome measures, precluded a meta-analysis of the data. Only one study reported the outcome of a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency. Three studies reported percentage reductions in seizure frequency compared to placebo. One study found an average seizure reduction of 35.8% with felbamate, while another reported a more modest reduction of 4.2%. Both studies noted that seizure frequency increased with placebo and that the difference in seizure reduction between felbamate and placebo was statistically significant (P = 0.0005 and P = 0.018, respectively). A third study reported a 14% reduction in seizure frequency with felbamate but found no significant difference between treatments. The results regarding treatment withdrawal were inconsistent. One study reported higher withdrawal rates for participants randomized to placebo, while the other three studies reported higher withdrawal rates for those randomized to felbamate. However, across all four studies, the treatment withdrawal rates for felbamate remained relatively low (less than 10%), suggesting that the drug may be well tolerated. The most common reason for withdrawal among felbamate-treated participants was adverse effects. The adverse effects most frequently reported in the felbamate-treated groups were headache, dizziness, and nausea. These side effects were observed in 23% to 40% of felbamate-treated participants, compared to 3% to 15% of those receiving placebo. The evidence for all outcomes was assessed using the GRADE approach and was rated as very low certainty. This low confidence in the findings was primarily due to imprecision, the narrative synthesis of the data, and the small number of events reported. It is emphasized that the true effect of felbamate may differ significantly from the findings of this review. In conclusion, due to methodological limitations, the small number of included studies, and variability in outcome measures, there is no reliable evidence to support the use of felbamate as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal-onset epilepsy. A large-scale, randomized controlled trial conducted over a longer duration is necessary to provide more definitive guidance for clinical practice.
